subject: [PATCH RFC v4 12/12] selftests/mm: add a slow-GUP content and COW test for mTHP

reviews.author: Mike Rapoport
reviews.summary:
Reviewer noted that the test does not handle the case where the mTHP is split across multiple PTEs, which would cause the slow GUP path to return incorrect pages.

Reviewer Mike Rapoport requested that the test code use ksft_* helpers for printing messages and tracking failed and passed tests, suggesting improvements to the test's logging and reporting functionality.
reviews.raw_body:
Hi Rik,

On Fri, Jul 24, 2026 at 06:29:34PM -0400, Rik van Riel wrote:

---

Please (instruct claude to) use ksft_* helpers for printing messages and
tracking failed and passed tests.

2026-07-26.patch_summary: This patch adds a new test, mthp_gup_cow_test, to the Linux kernel selftests suite. The test checks that the slow get_user_pages() path correctly handles large folios (mTHP) and copy-on-write (COW) operations. It does this by pinning a region of memory on the slow path, writing a distinct pattern to each page, and then verifying that the kernel copies back the correct contents from the pinned pages after a COW operation. The test also reports how many pages are in contiguous large-folio runs, allowing for better coverage testing of kernels without mTHP support.

reviews.author: David (Arm)
reviews.summary: Reviewer David expressed strong disagreement with the patch, citing its implementation as 'AI slop' that violates current mm selftest standards and instead suggested extending existing tests to naturally test mTHP.
reviews.raw_body:
I'm sorry, I cannot be convinced to review this AI slop here. You should have
known better to no send such a ... patch ... out.

It completely violates to how we are supposed to write mm selftests in 2026.

Also, testing some implementation details is not really what we want.

Extend other tests to just naturally test mthp as well, please, if they don't
already do that.

Having a separate selftest just for this is just extremely ... odd.

-- 
Cheers,

David

reviews.author: David (Arm)
reviews.summary: Reviewer David (Arm) expressed frustration that the patch requires reviewers to review AI-generated code, citing a lack of time and requesting that contributors take full responsibility for their contributions.
reviews.raw_body:
I'm afraid we won't have time to keep repeating the following:

Documentation/process/coding-assistants.rst

* Reviewing all AI-generated code
[...]
* Taking full responsibility for the contribution

-- 
Cheers,

David

reviews.author: Rik Riel (author)
reviews.summary: Author acknowledged a mistake in their code review process and plans to improve it by adding LLM rules to catch generalizable mistakes, ensuring others can avoid repeating the same errors.
reviews.raw_body:
I did review the code. I missed this one, largely
because I was focused more on the mm bits.

Not only will I clean it up, I will also make sure
that other people using the available Linux kernel
AI tooling will automatically avoid repeating this
mistake.

I submitted some self test checks to review-prompts:

https://github.com/masoncl/review-prompts/pull/89

And added some commits to kernel-style to create
clearer comments:

https://github.com/rikvanriel/kernel-style

I also tested the patch series against the updated
review-prompts and kernel-style guidelines, and
the issues that were pointed got caught with
the updated tooling.


With the gigablock patch series, I tried to edit
the default LLM output, and create something
vaguely decent. That was a lost cause, which I
do not plan to repeat. 

It was an especially big waste of time with the 
code that I was never planning to keep, but where 
I had not thought of an alternative approach yet.

The current plan of attack is to add LLM rules
every time I get a comment on a patch series
that addresses something generalizable that
I missed.

That way anybody using those tools should have
those mistakes caught, and either raised or
fixed by tooling, before they even start
editing their code.

You don't want to review the same mistakes
over and over again, and I want to help
people avoid sending the same mistakes that
were previously made.

-- 
All Rights Reversed.
